title: Cards vs. Local Payment Methods in Southeast Asia: What Merchants Should Know
summary: Compare cards and local payment methods in Southeast Asia to build a market-specific payment mix that improves conversion.
body_markdown:
Cards remain a significant payment method across Southeast Asia, and businesses entering the region need to accept card payments to maximize their customer reach. However, customers in each market also have their own preferred ways to pay, so merchants need to compare cards vs. local payment methods in Southeast Asia for every market they enter.


[Regional e-commerce data](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) shows why this comparison matters. Southeast Asia's e-commerce payment value is


**projected to reach $325.3B in 2028** , with


**domestic payments** at $97.9B,


**mobile wallets** at $94.9B, and


**cards** at $93.9B. Domestic payments here refer to real-time payments and local bank-based payment schemes.


With payment value spread almost evenly across these three categories, neither cards nor local payment methods can represent how the region pays on their own. For your business, a checkout built around only one category of payment method leaves a large share of regional payment value outside it.


To capture that value, your business needs to offer


**the right combination** of cards and local payment methods in each market it serves. That combination determines how many ready-to-buy customers can complete their payment, and in turn how much


**revenue** your business earns in each country.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- Where cards fit in a regional payment strategy, and why merchant acceptance and customer usage can point in different directions


- Why local payment methods such as QRIS, PromptPay, DuitNow, and PayNow carry a growing share of e-commerce value


- The five factors that shape the right payment mix for each market


- What to look for in a regional payment setup, and the risks of offering too few payment methods


- How Xendit combines cards and local payment methods through one integration


The analysis starts with cards, since most merchants already accept them and they still cover needs that local methods cannot.


## **Where card payments in Southeast Asia fit into your payment strategy**


Cards matter in a regional checkout for two reasons, but one limitation affects how much your business should rely on them:


### **Cards remain important for cross-border and international customers**


Cards give customers a familiar way to pay a business based outside their home market. Card networks are built for


**global use** , while most local payment methods only support domestic transactions. A customer in Japan ordering from a retailer in Singapore, for example, will usually reach for a card.


This makes cards especially


**relevant for businesses** that serve a mix of the following customer groups:


- **Local customers** , who may hold a card alongside the local method they use most


- **Regional customers** , who buy across Southeast Asian borders and may not have a payment app from the merchant's market


- **International customers** , who pay from outside the region and depend on globally accepted card networks


Cards also carry most e-commerce spending in the region's most card-heavy market. In Singapore,


[cards accounted for 71%](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) of e-commerce transaction value in 2023, supported by a


**credit card penetration rate of 80%** , the highest in Southeast Asia. In practice, card acceptance works as the core of checkout in Singapore and as the cross-border option in markets where local methods lead.


### **Cards are the most widely accepted payment method among merchants**


In 2024,


**credit and debit cards** were the most widely accepted payment category among merchants


[in each of these markets](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) :


- **Indonesia** : 71% of merchants


- **Malaysia** : 81% of merchants


- **Philippines** : 86% of merchants


- **Singapore** : 86% of merchants


- **Thailand** : 79% of merchants


- **Vietnam** : 86% of merchants


This makes card acceptance the baseline for broad payment accessibility. A checkout without cards would fall short of what customers expect to find at most merchants in the region.


### **Card acceptance does not always match how customers pay**


The number of merchants accepting a payment method does not always show how many customers actually pay with it. In Indonesia, for example, credit and debit cards were the


**most widely accepted** online payment option among merchants, even though


**card penetration stood at just**[5%](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) in 2023.


The same gap appears in reverse for local methods. In Thailand, only 29% of surveyed merchants accepted real-time or QR payments and 37% accepted bank transfers, while domestic payments (24%) and mobile wallets (29%) together made up more than half of the country's e-commerce transaction value in 2023. In Vietnam, 35% of merchants accepted QR payments, even though 62% of Vietnamese consumers were already paying by QR in 2023.


Accepting cards gives your business broad reach, but


**card acceptance alone does not mean your payment setup reflects how local customers pay** . The gap between what checkouts offer and what customers use is a conversion opportunity for merchants, because the methods customers rely on most are often the ones checkouts still leave out.


Closing that gap starts with understanding why customers favor local methods so strongly, beginning with the payment infrastructure each country has built.


## **Why local payment methods in Southeast Asia matter for merchants**


Three developments explain why


**local payment methods** matter to merchants, and each one shapes how retailers should build checkout:


### **Southeast Asia has built strong domestic payment ecosystems**


Southeast Asian markets have built their payment infrastructure around


**local financial systems** , and each major market now runs on a


**national payment** rail or QR standard:


- **Indonesia** :


[QRIS](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/qris) (Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard), a single national QR code that customers can pay from any participating banking or e-wallet app


- **Thailand** :


[PromptPay](https://www.xendit.co/en-th/blog/accepting-mobile-banking-payments-in-thailand-a-complete-guide-for-businesses/) , a real-time payment system introduced by the Bank of Thailand in 2016 that links a bank account to a mobile number or citizen ID


- **Malaysia** :


[DuitNow](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/duitnow-pay) , the national real-time transfer and QR payment service used across banks and e-wallets


- **Singapore** :


[PayNow](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payment-channel-page-push-14) , which lets customers make instant bank transfers by scanning a QR code with a participating banking or e-wallet app


- **Philippines** :


[QR Ph](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/qr-ph-payments-in-the-philippines-a-business-guide-to-the-countrys-national-qr-standard/) , the unified national QR standard, alongside the InstaPay and PESONet transfer rails, where transfers grew


[33%](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) in Q1 2024 compared with 2023


- **Vietnam** : VietQR, which recorded


[more than 100 million transactions](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) per month in Q1 2024


These networks connect directly to local banking infrastructure, which reduces intermediaries and speeds up processing, and governments actively promote them to widen financial inclusion and lower transaction costs. For merchants, that backing has made local methods part of everyday payment behavior in each market, so customers expect to see them at checkout.


### **Consumer adoption is driven by local payment preferences**


Across the region, local payment methods are widely used, and customers choose them for similar reasons:


- **Indonesia** :


[94% of respondents](https://dataindonesia.id/keuangan/detail/hasil-survei-alasan-warga-indonesia-menggunakan-layanan-qris) use QRIS, with 49% citing ease of use and 42% citing transaction speed as their reasons


- **Thailand** : PromptPay had


[77.2 million registrations](https://juspay.io/en-sg/blog/promptpay-reshaping-thailand-s-financial-landscape) as of December 2023 and processed 2.16 billion transactions in September 2025 alone, with users drawn to its convenience, security, and the ability to pay through familiar identifiers such as a mobile number


- **Malaysia** :


[69% of respondents](https://www.mfpc.org.my/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/CMDF-2024-Completed-Version1.pdf) use DuitNow, ahead of Touch 'n Go at 68% and ShopeePay at 64%, and they cite security, convenience, and faster transactions as the main advantages of digital wallets


- **Singapore** :


[83% of surveyed consumers](https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/2026/04/payment-methods/index.html) use PayNow, second only to credit and debit cards at 87%, and 54% describe digital payments as convenient, the leading reason for using them


**Convenience** and


**speed** appear in every market. Local methods work inside the banking and wallet apps customers already use, so paying requires no card details and fewer steps. A customer who can pay inside an app they open every day has fewer reasons to stop before the payment is complete.


### **Local payment methods carry a growing share of e-commerce value**


Adoption at this scale shows up in


**online spending** . In 2023, cards were still the largest single


[e-commerce payment category in Southeast Asia](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) at $40.8B, slightly ahead of


**domestic payments** at $38.9B and


**mobile wallets** at $35.4B. Together, those two local categories already accounted for more than half of the region's e-commerce payment value that year, and each of them


**is expected to overtake cards by 2028** .


Cards will keep growing in absolute value, so they remain relevant. The risk for merchants is a card-only strategy, which is built around less than 30% of the region's e-commerce payment value and leaves the rest of the opportunity uncovered.


### **What this means for retailers**


Customers across Southeast Asia arrive at checkout with payment habits already formed by their local banks and wallet apps. Retailers operating across the region therefore need to start from the methods customers use in each market, instead of assuming one payment method mix will work everywhere.


The commercial return is measurable. Businesses that offer local payment methods see an average


[12% increase in revenue and a 7.4% boost in conversion](https://www.ppro.com/insights/retail-payments-why-local-payment-methods-drive-global-conversion/) rates. For a retailer, that uplift comes from customers who already intended to buy and needed a familiar way to pay.


***Also read:***[E-Commerce Payment Strategy in Southeast Asia: Winning on Conversion, Reliability, and Scale](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/e-commerce-payment-strategy-in-southeast-asia-winning-on-conversion-reliability-and-scale/)


Knowing that local methods matter still leaves the practical decision of which ones to offer in each market and what role cards should play alongside them. That decision depends on both the market and the business.


## **Why merchants need a market-specific payment method mix**


Instead of ranking cards against local methods, merchants should evaluate the combination of methods for each market they operate in, with


**five factors shaping the right payment method mix** for each market:


### **Customer profile**


Start with who pays you. Are your customers mainly local, regional, or international?


**International customers** are more likely to rely on cards, while


**domestic customers** often already have a preferred local method. A retailer with a large overseas customer base needs strong card acceptance in every market, while a business selling mainly to domestic shoppers should build its checkout around local methods first.


### **Market payment behavior**


Next, identify which payment methods carry


**meaningful transaction volume in each market** and which local payment method customers already use.


[IDC's market data](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) shows how much the answer changes between countries:


- **Malaysia** : Domestic payments, led by bank transfers, were the largest e-commerce payment category in 2023 at 38% of transaction value, while mobile wallets are set to gain the most share, rising 6 percentage points by 2028


- **Philippines** : Cash-based and other alternative methods such as cash on delivery still made up 30% of e-commerce value in 2023, and mobile wallets led the digital categories at 24%, in a market where 44% of the population was unbanked in 2021


- **Vietnam** : Mobile wallets are projected to overtake both cards and domestic payments as the leading online payment method by 2028


Each market therefore needs its own


**shortlist of priority** methods, because the leading option in one country can be a minor one next door.


### **Transaction context**


Different payment methods suit different


**purchasing situations** . A merchant may need cards for international customers while relying on bank transfers, e-wallets, or QR payments for domestic orders.


**Order value** matters too, since many local methods carry per-transaction limits set by the scheme or provider, which can push high-value orders toward methods with higher ceilings, such as bank transfers or virtual accounts.


**Devices** also change the flow. On desktop, a customer scans the QR code on screen with their banking app, while on a mobile browser, the customer typically saves the QR code as an image and opens it in their banking app to pay. Mapping methods to these situations helps your team decide which options to show first for each type of order and device.


### **Business model**


An e-commerce retailer, a marketplace, a subscription business, and a travel platform each need different things from their payment mix:


- **E-commerce** retailers need refund options that match their returns policy, since refund support varies between cards and many local methods


- **Marketplaces** collect from buyers through many methods at once and need transaction records clear enough to settle accurately with each seller


- **Subscription** businesses need methods that can save payment details and support charges the business initiates on schedule, which cards provide and many e-wallets and direct debit options now support as well


- **Travel** platforms serve international visitors who tend to default to cards and often need to reserve funds at booking and charge the final amount later


The right payment method mix therefore follows the customers and transaction flows your business actually serves.


***Also read:***[How to Choose the Right Subscription Payment Methods for Each Southeast Asian Market](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/how-to-choose-the-right-subscription-payment-methods-for-each-southeast-asian-market/)


### **Cost, settlement, and dispute exposure**


Cards and local methods also differ in


**what they cost** and


**how funds move** . Card processing combines interchange (the fee paid to the card-issuing bank), scheme, and acquirer fees, and card payments follow formal chargeback rules that let customers dispute a transaction through their bank. Local methods generally carry lower fees for domestic transactions, and chargebacks are rare or unavailable for many of them.


In Singapore, merchants spend an


[average of 1.5% to 3%](https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/2026/04/payment-methods/index.html) of each transaction on card processing fees, which help fund the cashback and rewards that make cards attractive to consumers. Many local methods also work as push payments, where the customer sends funds from their own banking or wallet app. Once authenticated, these payments are difficult to reverse, which lowers exposure to friendly fraud, where a customer disputes a purchase they actually made.


For your finance team, the payment mix is also a margin and cash flow decision, so each method's cost, settlement timing, and dispute exposure should be modeled before a market goes live.


There is no universal payment method mix for Southeast Asia. The strongest setup combines the international reach of cards with the local relevance of each market's preferred methods. Running that setup across several markets depends on the infrastructure behind your checkout, so the next step is knowing what to look for in it.


## **What merchants should look for in a regional payment setup**


Before choosing or expanding payment methods, merchants should


**test** their


**payment setup** against these five questions:


### **Payment coverage**


Does the setup support both international cards and the locally preferred methods in every market you serve?


Coverage should include the major card networks alongside each market's national QR standard, leading e-wallets, and bank transfer or direct debit options. Your payment provider should also show


[the transaction limits, settlement time, and refund support for each payment channel](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) , so your team can compare coverage against your own customer data and spot where customers are still missing their preferred option.


### **Market flexibility**


Can your business adjust its payment mix from one market to another without rebuilding the integration? Payment preferences change at each border, so your team should be able to switch methods on for each market as results come in.


In a well-designed


[payments API](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-payments-api-work) , adding a method means passing a different channel code in the same payment request, with no new connection to build. That flexibility lets your payment mix keep improving after launch instead of staying fixed.


### **Integration**


Can multiple payment methods run through one consistent technical connection? Payment methods complete in different ways. E-wallets and online banking usually redirect the customer to authenticate, QR codes and virtual accounts present a code the customer pays separately, and saved payment methods can complete with no customer action.


One integration should handle all three flows and return a consistent status for each payment, with real-time confirmation sent to your systems through


[webhooks](https://docs.xendit.co/v1/docs/handling-webhooks) . Your engineering team then maintains one set of logic for payment status and order updates across every method.


### **Operational visibility**


Can finance and operations teams monitor payment activity across methods and markets? Every method you add brings its own fees, settlement timing, and refund rules.


Your teams need one


[transactions report](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) that covers every method and market in the same format, with


[reports](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reports-overview) delivered automatically instead of assembled by hand from several dashboards. With that view, your team can compare cards and local methods side by side and reconcile them in one process.


### **Scalability**


Can new payment methods and markets be added as the business grows? Collecting and settling payments in a new country means operating under that country's payment regulations.


A provider that holds


[local payment licenses](https://www.xendit.co/en/company/xendit-licenses/) across the region can add markets to your existing setup, while a provider without them may leave your team arranging a separate local partner for each expansion. Licensing depth decides whether the next market is a quick activation or a new procurement and integration project.


***Also read:***[What to Look for in a Payment Partner When Expanding from the US to Southeast Asia](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/what-to-look-for-payment-partner-expanding-us-to-southeast-asia/)


Setups that fall short on these questions tend to fail in a few predictable ways, and each one costs revenue or engineering time.


## **The risks of offering too few payment methods in Southeast Asia**


[A checkout with limited payment options creates three problems](https://www.ppro.com/insights/retail-payments-why-local-payment-methods-drive-global-conversion/) for merchants selling across Southeast Asia:


### **Customers may not find the payment method they prefer**


A customer can reach the checkout ready to buy and still leave because the method they normally use is missing. Research shows that 10% of shoppers have abandoned a checkout because the payment methods they wanted were not available. That loss happens at the most expensive point in the funnel, after your marketing has already paid to bring the customer to checkout.


***Also read:***[How Payment Success Rates Turn Checkout Demand Into E-Commerce Revenue](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/how-payment-success-rates-turn-checkout-demand-into-e-commerce-revenue/)


### **International customers may need a different payment option**


A checkout built mainly around local methods can serve domestic customers well and still leave customers paying from another market without a workable option. Cross-border shoppers expect a familiar experience, with 99% wanting to pay through the methods they normally use, and 72% of merchants report higher failure rates on cross-border payments than on domestic ones.


A business selling both locally and across borders needs local methods for domestic customers and dependable card acceptance for everyone else.


### **Businesses can end up rebuilding payment coverage market by market**


Adding local methods one provider at a time creates several integrations and several operational workflows. Each market and payment method can come with its own settlement file, reporting format, and currency requirement, so every new market adds manual reconciliation work for finance teams. If your business adds local methods this way, it will end up with more complex payment operations in every new market, with your engineering team maintaining several connections and your finance team reconciling several sets of records.


***Also read:***[Scaling E-Commerce Payments Across Southeast Asia: Why Businesses Need Cross-Border Payment Infrastructure](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/scaling-e-commerce-payments-across-southeast-asia-why-businesses-need-cross-border-payment-infrastructure/)


The goal for merchants is the right coverage in each market, delivered without adding infrastructure complexity every time the payment method mix changes. Xendit brings card acceptance and local payment methods into one regional setup built around that goal.

## **FAQ for merchants in Southeast Asia: Cards and local payment methods**


### **Do I still need to accept credit cards if I offer local payment methods in Southeast Asia?**


Yes, most merchants need both. Cards serve international buyers and card-heavy markets such as Singapore, while


[local payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) serve domestic customers across the rest of the region. With


**Xendit** , card acceptance runs through the same integration as QR, e-wallet, and bank transfer payments, so your business can offer both without adding a second payment provider.


### **How long do card payments take to settle compared with QR and e-wallet payments?**


With


**Xendit,**[card payments settle on T+5 business days, while QRIS and most e-wallets settle on T+2 business days](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) . Some local methods settle almost immediately, including PromptPay in Thailand and several Indonesian virtual accounts such as BRI, BNI, and Mandiri. Business-day timelines exclude weekends and public holidays, and Xendit's


[early settlement](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/early-settlement/) gives your business access to funds as soon as the customer pays.


### **Can PromptPay, QRIS, or virtual account payments be refunded?**


It depends on the channel. With


**Xendit** , cards support full and partial refunds for up to 365 days, QRIS supports full refunds within 30 days, and GCash supports refunds for up to 180 days, while PromptPay, virtual accounts, FPX, and over-the-counter payments do not support refunds through the original payment route. For those channels, your business can return funds through


[Xendit Payout Links](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/xenpayout/) , which send money to the customer without your team collecting their account details in advance.


### **Can I use e-wallets or direct debit instead of cards for recurring payments?**


Yes. Many local methods on


**Xendit** support saved payment details and merchant-initiated charges, including OVO, DANA, ShopeePay, and GoPay in Indonesia, Maya and GrabPay in the Philippines, Touch 'n Go in Malaysia, and direct debit with major Thai banks.


[Xendit Subscriptions](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/subscriptions/) collects payments on your schedule across these methods and cards, so recurring billing can follow how customers in each market prefer to pay.


### **Can international customers pay with PromptPay, QRIS, or other local payment methods?**


PromptPay payments come from a Thai bank account and QRIS payments come from participating banking and e-wallet apps, which most online buyers outside the region do not have. Cross-border QR links, such as PromptPay's connections with PayNow, DuitNow, and QRIS, mainly serve travelers paying merchants in person and person-to-person transfers. For international online buyers,


**Xendit** supports international card acceptance in each of its markets, along with


[multi-currency card processing](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/card-multi-currency-processing) in markets including Singapore, Hong Kong, and the Philippines.


### **Which costs less for merchants in Southeast Asia, cards or local payment methods?**


It depends on the market and the method, so the comparison needs to be made channel by channel.


**Xendit** has its


[fees for every payment method](https://www.xendit.co/en/pricing/) by market, including separate rates for domestic and international cards, and the


[billing report](https://docs.xendit.co/v1/docs/billing-report) breaks down the fees charged on each transaction. Your finance team can use both to weigh what each method costs against the conversion it brings.
